papers.what_it_is: An empirical study comparing SVM, KNN, RF, bagging, boosting, LR and a voting ensemble (two variants) for credit card fraud detection on the public European ULB dataset, using under-sampling and SMOTE, with accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC and timing/RAM measurements.

assertions.value: The authors use the Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset of transactions by European cardholders over two days, with 492 frauds among 284,807 transactions (a 0.172% positive class).
quotes: The dataset contained records of transactions conducted by European credit cardholders over two days.
In the dataset, there were 492 instances of fraud out of a total of 284,807 transactions during the specified time frame.
with the positive class (frauds) representing only 0.172% of all transactions.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own dataset setup in Section 3.1.
assertions.reader_inference: Single public dataset only; results do not show generalisation to other issuers, years or fraud types.

assertions.value: The authors state that the 28 features V1-V28 were transformed with PCA for confidentiality, while the Time and Amount features were not altered.
quotes: Each transaction in the dataset was associated with 28 additional features labelled as V1–V28.
Due to confidentiality concerns, these features were transformed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
It is important to note that the ‘Time’ and ‘Amount’ features were exceptions to this transformation; PCA did not alter them.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper describes the dataset it uses.

assertions.value: The authors report pre-processing that standardised the Amount column, removed the Time column and checked for and removed duplicate entries.
quotes: Standardising the ‘Amount’ column to make it easy for analysis.
Removing the ‘Time’ Column from the dataset as it was not contributing much during
Checking and removing duplicate entries in the dataset.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own pre-processing setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The legitimate count falls from 284,315 to 275,190 and fraud from 492 to 473, which suggests duplicate removal dropped roughly 9,000 rows.

assertions.value: The authors state that feature selection techniques were not used because the dataset gives no information about its features.
quotes: Therefore, the use of feature selection techniques was not possible because it would have required clear visibility of feature information.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this scope limit themselves.

assertions.value: The authors state that no intentional action was taken to reduce the influence of outliers, because the chosen models were considered naturally resistant to outliers.
quotes: It is important to mention that intentional actions to reduce the influence of outliers were not included.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own pre-processing choice.
assertions.reader_inference: Robustness to outliers is asserted, not tested.

assertions.value: The authors report that after pre-processing the dataset comprised 275,190 legitimate entries and 473 fraud-labelled entries.
quotes: After pre-processing, the dataset comprised 275,190 legitimate entries and 473 fraud-labelled entries, indicating a significant skewness for model training.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own data counts.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 3.1 uses the raw counts (492 fraud, 284,315 legitimate); later sizes (e.g. 220,152 per class in the SMOTE training sample) follow the post-processing counts.

assertions.value: The authors balanced the data by randomly choosing a sample of legitimate transactions equal in number to the minority (fraud) class and concatenating both classes.
quotes: In this paper, for better model training, the entries for both classes were made equal by choosing a random sample equal
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper describes its own sampling procedure.
assertions.reader_inference: With about 473 fraud cases the under-sampled dataset is under 1,000 rows, so test-set metrics rest on few cases.

assertions.value: The authors oversampled the fraud class with SMOTE until it equalled the legitimate class, then merged both classes into one dataset.
quotes: So, for SMOTE, the fraud class (labelled as 1) was oversampled, equal to the legit class to have identical entries for each class to train models optimally.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper describes its own sampling procedure.
assertions.reader_inference: Sampling is described and drawn (Figure 1) as happening before the train/test split; the SMOTE test set has equal class counts (55,038 per class by Table 8) and 110,076 entries, twice the legitimate count split 80/20. This indicates synthetic fraud rows in the test set and possible leakage, so SMOTE test metrics are probably optimistic.

assertions.value: The authors report a SMOTE training sample of 440,304 entries and a testing sample of 110,076 entries.
quotes: These confusion matrices represent the results of predictions for 440,304 entries or values present in the training sample.
According to the results obtained from the testing sample of 110,076 entries, which were unknown entries to machine learning models
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own sample sizes.
assertions.reader_inference: The two sizes sum to 550,380, twice 275,190, so the split is 80/20 of a fully balanced SMOTE dataset.

assertions.value: The authors describe the ensemble as SVM, KNN, RF, Bagging, Adaboost and a voting classifier, with KNN and RF as the base classifiers of Bagging and Boosting at default settings.
quotes: The ensemble combined Support Vector Machines (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest (RF), Bagging, Adaboost, and a voting classifier.
Since Bagging and Boosting are ensemble algorithms, KNN and RF were used as base classifiers with their default settings.
an ensemble model that integrates SVM, KNN, RF, Bagging, and Boosting classifiers within a voting framework.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its proposed model in Section 3.2 and restates it in the conclusion.
assertions.reader_inference: The voting rule (hard or soft, weights) is not specified in the text.

assertions.value: The authors define two proposed-model variants: P_M_1 uses SVM and P_M_2 uses logistic regression, and P_M_2 is the same model as PM (SMOTE) with a different sampling technique.
quotes: The proposed model with SVM (P_M_1) ranked third, with 24 false predictions for positive class values.
According to these findings, the second proposed model with LR (P_M_2)
The P_M_2 is the same model as PM; the only difference is the sampling technique used for the dataset.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the variants and their relation (also Figure 2).
assertions.reader_inference: The SMOTE tables report PM and LR but no SVM or P_M_1, although the SMOTE ROC discussion names SVM.

assertions.value: The authors report testing SVM regularisation values from 1.0 to 10 with linear, poly and rbf kernels, KNN neighbours from 2.0 to 10, and RF estimators from 10 to 100, and state that default parameters gave the best results.
quotes: testing different regularisation values ranging from 1.0 to 10 and various kernels such as linear, poly, and rbf.
Similarly, KNN and RF were examined using various values for n-neighbors (ranging from 2.0 to 10) and n-estimators (ranging from 10 to 100).
The analysis showed that the default parameters produced the best outcomes.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical tuning observation from one study; the data used to choose configurations is not stated.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says the best efficiency occurred 'during both the training and testing phases', and no validation set is mentioned, so tuning may have used the test data.

assertions.value: The authors define precision as TP over TP plus FP, recall as the ratio of correctly predicted positive observations to total actual positive observations, and F1 as the combination of precision and recall.
quotes: Precision is the ratio of TP to all positive predictions (TP + FP) made by a model.
It is the ratio of correctly predicted positive observations to the total actual positive observations.
F1-score is a metric used to combine the results of precision and recall into a single value.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its evaluation metrics.
assertions.reader_inference: In Tables 5, 6, 11 and 13 recall equals accuracy exactly, so the reported precision, recall and F1 look class-weighted averages rather than fraud-class values; the averaging method is not stated.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the under-sampled training sample RF and boosting made no false positive or false negative predictions, and the ACC of RF and Boosting is 100%.
quotes: Based on the provided results, both RF and boosting models exhibited 0 false positive and false negative values, indicating accurate predictions for both classes.
Similar to the results of the confusion matrix for training samples, the ACC of RF and Boosting models is 100%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one run on training data.
assertions.reader_inference: Perfect training accuracy with lower test accuracy (about 0.937 for RF) shows overfitting, although the authors call the models 'optimally fitted'.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the under-sampled testing sample the second proposed model (P_M_2, LR-based) and bagging outperformed all other models, with ten values predicted falsely (8 FP, 2 FN).
quotes: According to these findings, the second proposed model with LR (P_M_2) and bagging outperformed all other models, with ten values predicted falsely (8 FP, 2 FN).
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one run on a 190-entry test set.
assertions.reader_inference: On 190 test entries one error is about 0.5 percentage points, and the other models make 11 to 15 errors (Table 3); no repeated runs or intervals are reported, so the margin is within plausible noise.

quotes: (P_M_2) emerges as the most proficient among all models in predicting the positive class
achieving precision, recall, and an F1-score of 95%.
